extract

/ik-STRAKT/ — rhymes with "attract" · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To extract something is to carefully pull or draw it out from the place where it is embedded or contained.

The dentist extracted the cracked tooth in minutes.

Worked Example

The archaeologist carefully extracted the fossilized bone from the rock surrounding it using delicate tools and hours of patience.

Extract implies careful, deliberate removal from something that holds it tightly. Just saying "dug out" or "removed" wouldn't capture the precision needed when an item is embedded in another material.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

remove: To remove something is simply to take it away from where it is — the word covers everything from lifting a plate off a table to deleting a name from a list. To extract is a special kind of removing: drawing something out of a place that holds it tightly, where care and precision matter.

withdraw: To withdraw something is to take it back out smoothly and deliberately, usually reversing your own action — a hand from a pocket, savings from an account, an offer from the table. To extract points at the grip of the place instead: the thing is stuck or embedded, and freeing it takes careful work.

retrieve: To retrieve something is to go after it and bring it back to where it belongs — a librarian retrieves a folder from the archives. The word cares about recovering the thing itself. To extract cares about the tight spot it sits in and the careful pulling that works it free.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

insert: to put something into a place

embed: to fix something firmly deep inside

Where it sits · how completely it comes out — tug → pull → extract → wrench

tug vs. extract: Tug is far weaker than extract — a tug is just a quick little pull, while to extract is to draw something all the way out of the place where it is stuck.

pull vs. extract: Pull is weaker than extract; pulling is any ordinary drawing motion, while extracting means carefully pulling something completely out of where it is embedded.

wrench vs. extract: Wrench is stronger than extract — extracting removes something with careful effort, but wrenching yanks it out with sudden, violent force.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — ex-

Prefix — ex-: out of (Latin)

Root — tract

Root — tract: to pull, drag (from trahere/tractus) (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Ex- ('out of') plus tract ('to pull, drag') literally spells out the meaning: to extract something is to drag it out of the place where it is stuck or contained.

Use the root in a new word: tractor

Use the root in a new word: tractor: A tractor is a machine built to pull heavy loads — the same root tract, 'to pull,' that makes extract mean to pull something out.

Word Choice

neutral / formal

Extract suggests careful, deliberate removal of something embedded or contained. Use it when precision and tightness matter — like removing teeth, fossils, or specific information. For simple pulling, "pull" is clearer.
